title: BGP-4 Path-Vector Routing & Autonomous Systems

source_sentences.text: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP-4) is the standardized exterior gateway routing protocol facilitating policy-driven inter-domain traffic routing across autonomous systems (AS) on the global Internet backbone.

Unlike interior gateway protocols such as OSPF that calculate shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm across a uniform metric space, BGP functions as a path-vector protocol exchanging Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) over reliable Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) peering sessions on destination port 179.

BGP border routers actively suppress routing loops by evaluating the mandatory AS_PATH attribute; if a router identifies its own autonomous system number (ASN) within the advertised sequence of traversed systems, the routing update is immediately discarded.

Best-path determination evaluates advertised routes through a deterministic hierarchy of path attributes, sequentially prioritizing highest Local Preference (LOCAL_PREF), shortest AS_PATH hop length, lowest origin code, and lowest Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED) before evaluating interior gateway protocol tiebreakers.

preserved_terms.definition: The standard path-vector routing protocol used to exchange routing information between autonomous systems on the Internet.
A collection of connected IP routing prefixes under the control of one or more network operators (like an ISP or tech company).
Open Shortest Path First: an interior gateway routing protocol used within a single local network.
A graph search algorithm that solves the single-source shortest path problem for non-negative edge costs.
Network Layer Reachability Information: the IP prefixes and subnet lengths being advertised in BGP updates.
The standard transmission control protocol port used for reliable BGP peering sessions.
An ordered list of autonomous system numbers that a route advertisement has passed through, used for loop detection.
Autonomous System Number: a unique globally recognized identifier assigned to each autonomous network.
Local Preference: a BGP path attribute indicating preferred outbound exit paths from an autonomous system.
Multi-Exit Discriminator: an attribute suggesting to external neighbors which inbound entry link is preferred.

expert.text: BGP-4 is the standardized exterior gateway protocol orchestrating policy-based inter-domain traffic exchange among autonomous systems across the Internet.
Diverging from link-state IGPs using Dijkstra's algorithm, BGP operates as a path-vector protocol distributing NLRI over persistent TCP sessions on port 179.
Border routers prevent routing loops by verifying the AS_PATH attribute, unconditionally dropping advertisements containing their own ASN.
Deterministic path selection systematically evaluates LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH length, origin type, and MED metrics prior to IGP tiebreakers.

grade10.text: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP-4) is the exterior gateway routing protocol connecting autonomous systems (AS—large independent networks like ISPs) across the global Internet.

Unlike interior gateway protocols such as OSPF (which calculates shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm), BGP functions as a path-vector protocol exchanging NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information—lists of reachable IP prefixes) over reliable TCP peering sessions on port 179.
BGP border routers prevent routing loops by checking the AS_PATH attribute; if a router finds its own ASN (Autonomous System Number) in the path sequence, the update is immediately discarded.

BGP determines best paths through a deterministic hierarchy of attributes: highest LOCAL_PREF (Local Preference), shortest AS_PATH hop length, lowest origin code, and lowest MED (Multi-Exit Discriminator).

grade6.text: The BGP-4 protocol connects large Autonomous Systems (AS networks) across the Internet.
BGP does not use internal protocols like OSPF or Dijkstra's algorithm to calculate shortest paths.
Instead, BGP works as a path-vector protocol exchanging NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information) over TCP on port 179.
Border routers stop routing loops by checking the AS_PATH attribute.
If a router spots its own ASN (Autonomous System Number) in the AS_PATH, it drops the route.
BGP chooses the best path using LOCAL_PREF (Local Preference), shortest AS_PATH length, and MED (Multi-Exit Discriminator).

glossary.plain: Border Gateway Protocol version 4: the core routing protocol of the global Internet.
A large network or collection of IP prefixes under a single administrative authority (like an ISP).
Open Shortest Path First: an internal routing protocol that maps links inside a single network.
A mathematical graph algorithm used by OSPF to compute the shortest route across network routers.
Network Layer Reachability Information: the IP prefixes and subnet masks advertised between routers.
The reliable communication channel used to maintain live BGP peering sessions.
The ordered list of network IDs that a route has visited, used to detect and prevent infinite loops.
A BGP metric configured inside an organization to choose which outbound exit point is favored.
Multi-Exit Discriminator: an attribute that suggests to outside peers which link into your network is preferred.

quiz.q: What transport layer protocol and destination port does BGP-4 utilize for peering sessions?
options: Raw IP packets without transport layer protocols
quiz.hint: Check sentence 2 for the reliable transport mechanism mentioned.
quiz.explanation: BGP establishes reliable peering sessions using TCP connections on destination port 179.

quiz.q: How does a BGP border router detect and prevent routing loops?
options: By setting a TTL counter to 15 hops
By inspecting the AS_PATH attribute and discarding routes containing its own ASN
By re-running Dijkstra's algorithm every 30 seconds
By encrypting the route with asymmetric SSL certificates
quiz.hint: Consider what happens if a router discovers its own network number in the traversed history.
quiz.explanation: If a router's own ASN appears in the AS_PATH sequence, it knows the packet would loop back and discards the update.

quiz.q: Which path attribute is prioritized first in standard BGP best-path determination?
quiz.hint: Look at the sequential hierarchy of attributes described in sentence 4.
quiz.explanation: BGP path selection begins by prioritizing the route with the highest LOCAL_PREF attribute.

quiz.q: How does BGP differ fundamentally from interior protocols like OSPF?
options: OSPF runs across the entire global Internet while BGP is only local
BGP is a policy-driven path-vector protocol rather than a link-state shortest-path algorithm
OSPF requires manual approval for every single packet
quiz.hint: Compare path-vector policy routing with Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm.
quiz.explanation: BGP operates across independent networks using path-vector policies rather than uniform metric link-state algorithms.

quiz.q: What does NLRI represent in BGP routing exchanges?
options: Network Layer Reachability Information (IP prefixes advertised)
quiz.hint: Refer to the glossary and sentence 2 discussing network layer reachability.
quiz.explanation: NLRI stands for Network Layer Reachability Information, denoting prefixes reachable through the advertising router.

diagram_alt_text: Network architecture diagram of BGP inter-domain routing: AS 100 advertises IP prefix 198.51.100.0/24 to AS 200, appending ASN 100 to AS_PATH. AS 200 propagates the prefix to AS 300 with AS_PATH [200, 100]. If AS 300 tries to announce this back to AS 100, AS 100 detects its own ASN (100) and drops the update to prevent a loop.
